items.title: The Raindrop Size Rule Behind Supernumerary Rainbows
items.body: A supernumerary rainbow isn't a trick of the eye so much as a trick of uniformity. It only forms when the falling water droplets are all nearly the same size and typically less than a millimeter across. When that condition holds, sunlight doesn't merely reflect from inside the raindrops — it interferes, the same wave phenomenon you get as ripples spreading on a pond after a stone is thrown in. The fainter extra arcs are an interference pattern, which is why they depend on a narrow droplet-size distribution rather than on the storm simply being large.

sources.title: ‘A Statement’ Review: Paul Rudd, Paul Giamatti And Superb Ensemble In Tom McCarthy’s Splendid Humanist Look At Climate Change – New York Film Festival

items.title: Tom McCarthy's 'A Statement' Revisits a 1980 Climate Conference
items.body: Tom McCarthy's new film, A Statement, centers on a 1980 Florida conference dealing with the effects of carbon dioxide emissions on the environment. The gathering brings together politicians, academics, scientists and environmentalists from around the U.S. to talk about the subject. Deadline's critic notes that on paper this sounds like a dense polemic, hardly the stuff of exciting moviemaking — and a room full of experts and officials debating emissions is a genuinely hard thing to set in motion on screen. That tension is the interesting part of the premise: the film is built on the conference, not on the catastrophe.

sources.title: Trump urges calls to Arkansas Sen. Tom Cotton in push for permanent daylight saving time

discussion.body: The concrete grievance in the pitch is the clock change — running all over houses, farms and workplaces twice a year, and often forgetting — while the extra hour of daylight is the promise attached to it.
Or read it the other way around: the extra hour is the headline offer, and the twice-yearly hassle is what makes the whole thing sound like common sense rather than a policy argument.

items.title: Trump's Case for Permanent Daylight Saving, Aimed at Tom Cotton
items.body: On social media, Trump argued that if Tom Cotton were putting Arkansas first, he would give the state an extra hour of daylight and spare residents from running all over their houses, farms, workplaces and everywhere else twice a year to change clocks they often forget to change. The argument amounts to staying on daylight time year-round, and it is framed as a test of whether Cotton puts Arkansas first rather than as a scheduling question. The twice-yearly reset, in that telling, is the grievance; the extra evening daylight is the reward.

sources.title: Pierre Le Gall’s Passionate Love Story ‘Flesh and Fuel’ Named Best Film at Zurich Film Festival

items.title: Zurich's Top Prize Goes to a Love Story That Premiered at Cannes
items.body: French director Pierre Le Gall's passionate love story, 'Flesh and Fuel,' took the Golden Eye, the top prize at the 22nd Zurich Film Festival, on Saturday. The film had its world premiere in Cannes' Critics' Week before arriving in Switzerland. The festival's documentary prize went to Pete Muller's 'Bucks Harbor,' which premiered at the Berlin Film Festival's Panorama section. Two films that started at other festivals, then, ended up sharing Zurich's top honours — a reminder that the autumn festival circuit is often where earlier premieres get a second look from juries rather than audiences.

sources.title: AI giants 'not being nearly careful enough,' warns outgoing OpenAI safety engineer

discussion.body: The nuclear and aviation comparison only bites if the safeguards are mandatory. Both of those industries are regulated by bodies that can stop operations, which is a different kind of arrangement from a voluntary pact with the companies being regulated.

Fair as a description of where things stand, but it's also possible a voluntary pact is a first step toward something with teeth. Voluntary agreements have preceded formal rulemaking in other industries, so the analogy may describe a destination rather than a current state of affairs.

items.title: A Former OpenAI Worker Wants AI Treated Like Aviation
items.body: Days after President Donald Trump signed a voluntary pact with artificial intelligence companies, a former OpenAI worker said the industry needs safeguards of the same kind applied to nuclear power or aviation, DW reports. That comparison is the argument, not a policy detail: nuclear plants and airlines operate under mandatory safety regimes with inspectors and the power to ground things, while a pact that companies sign voluntarily rests on their own restraint. The timing underscores the gap — one framework asks for commitments, the other assumes oversight.

items.title: Jerry Golod, Producer of 'Tales From the Darkside,' Dies at 87
items.body: Jerry Golod, the producer of the horror series “Tales From the Darkside,” died at his home in Rancho Mirage, California, on Wednesday after a brief battle with cancer, Variety reports. He was 87. Earlier in his career Golod worked as an executive at CBS and NBC; in the early 1980s he launched his own shop, JayGee Productions.

items.body: Ars Technica argues that we now have better ways to power economic growth—ways that are less environmentally damaging now and won't leave our descendants with a carbon debt that will be difficult to manage. sources.title: 'Anger in the streets': Tens of thousands protest in Spain over housing crisis

discussion.body: Fifty-plus demonstrations in one day looks less like a single mass rally than a movement organized city by city, at the local level.
Or one national movement coordinating many sites on the same afternoon. The count alone can't tell us which of those it is.

items.title: More than 50 protests in Spain after an emergency bill failed
items.body:
More than 50 protests took place across Spain on Saturday over the country's housing crisis, the BBC reports, after the government failed to get emergency legislation through parliament.

The sequencing is the notable part. The demonstrations followed a specific legislative failure rather than an election or a budget fight, and emergency legislation is the instrument a government reaches for when it wants speed. When it doesn't pass, the pressure has somewhere else to go — in this case, by the BBC's count, into more than fifty separate demonstrations in a single day.

sources.title: B.C. lawyer found to have misappropriated $117K from dementia-stricken client

items.title: A B.C. lawyer, his client's condo, and 75 per cent of her estate
items.body:
CBC reports that a B.C. lawyer, Leonard Hil Marriott, was found to have misappropriated $117,000 from a client with dementia. He also prepared documents to give himself 50 per cent ownership of the woman's condo and 75 per cent of her estate.

The second detail is the one that lingers. The paperwork meant to arrange her affairs was, on the finding CBC reports, being drawn up to arrange his stake in them — which is a different kind of misconduct from simply moving money out of an account, and a reminder of how much trust sits inside ordinary estate documents.

sources.title: Can the Cornell lawsuit force changes that make students safer?

items.title: A university's duty when prosecutors don't file charges
items.body:
In its reporting on the Cornell lawsuit, NPR draws out a distinction that tends to get blurred in public arguments about campus sexual assault: universities have responsibilities when students report an assault, even if prosecutors don't bring charges. Attorney Baine Kerr, who spoke with NPR about how those protections work, treats the criminal question and the institutional one as separate obligations.

The practical effect is that a case can close in a prosecutor's office and stay open on a campus — a different process, with a separate set of consequences for the people involved.

sources.title: ‘Behemoth!’ Review: Pedro Pascal Plays a Wayward Cellist in Tony Gilroy’s Movingly Atonal Character Study About How People Conduct Themselves
Will ‘Behemoth!’ Push Pedro Pascal Into Oscar Contention?

discussion.body: A title like Behemoth! sets an expectation of size. Calling the actual film smaller and stranger than that name is not a knock so much as a recalibration of what kind of movie this is.

The Oscar angle being floated is specifically about the Music Branch, not the Academy at large — which makes sense for a film built as a love letter to film music, and also means the conversation is about craft categories rather than Best Picture buzz.

items.title: Tony Gilroy's 'Behemoth!' Promises More Than It Delivers on Name Alone
items.body: Tony Gilroy, best known lately as the creator of Andor, has returned to the big screen with a film that IndieWire describes as smaller and stranger than its title would suggest. Pedro Pascal is front and center in what the outlet calls a love letter to film music — and where a movie called Behemoth! might suggest scale, the review's framing is of something more intimate and off-kilter instead. The awards chatter has already narrowed to a specific gate: whether the Academy's Music Branch will embrace The Behemoth! Collective. That is a narrower question than general Oscar contention, and a more interesting one for a film whose central subject is music itself.

sources.title: Life on a hair trigger

discussion.body: If minds are part of how violence sustains itself, the usual split between fixing conditions and treating people stops being a split. On this framing they are the same project, approached from different ends.

There is a hazard in that frame. Talking about 'the minds it creates' can slide from explaining a violent world into diagnosing the people living in it, which is not the same claim and lands differently on the people concerned.

items.title: Violence Sustains Itself Through the Minds It Creates
items.body: The material account of a violent society is familiar: guns, poverty and other social ills. Writing in Aeon, Megan Kang adds a less tangible item to the list — the minds that violence creates. Her framing puts psychology inside the machinery rather than at the receiving end of it. A world of violence, on this account, does not merely injure people and move on; it produces a population shaped by that world, and that shaping is part of what keeps the whole thing running. Guns and deprivation remain central. The addition is that the supply of those conditions is not the only thing that has to be replenished.

sources.title: Why long-brewing physical and mental breakdowns feel so sudden

items.title: The Parallel a Neurosurgeon Sees Between Tumours and Strained Minds
items.body: Sasi S Senga writes in Psyche from two positions at once — neurosurgeon and son — and says that combination has led him to see parallel processes underlying growing tumours and stressed-out minds. The pairing is worth pausing on. One belongs to oncology, the other to mental health, and they are usually discussed in entirely separate registers. Senga's move is to notice the shared shape: something building underneath, whatever name the department gives it.
